beats.text: There are two main designs you'll meet. A solution calorimeter is an insulated cup with a lid, used for reactions that happen in solution, such as neutralisation or dissolving.

A bomb calorimeter is used for combustion. The fuel or food sample sits inside a sealed steel container, the bomb, filled with excess oxygen under pressure. A current through an ignition wire starts the combustion, and the heat passes through the steel into a measured amount of water around it, all inside an insulated jacket.

Because the bomb is sealed and well insulated, combustion is complete and very little heat escapes, so it gives much more accurate values than burning a fuel under a can of water. But in both designs, the water isn't the only thing that heats up, so both need a calibration factor.

The design also tells you which errors to look for. With an open cup, or a fuel burned under a can, heat escaping to the surroundings is the main problem, and an open flame may burn incompletely. A sealed, insulated bomb reduces both, which is why it's used to measure energy values for fuels and foods.
